The Eurasian oystercatcher (Haematopus ostralegus) is a large, conspicuous shorebird whose life history traits reflect its occupation of intertidal habitats. During the breeding season, females exhibit a maximum adult body mass approaching 480 grams [Wwi = 480 grams], which is comparable to that of other large charadriiforms. Newly hatched chicks emerge at a relatively low wet weight at birth of approximately 32 grams [Wwb = approximately 32 grams], a value that underscores the semi-precocial developmental mode typical of the Haematopodidae. The incubation period, which proceeds at a mean temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts for a duration ranging from 24 to 27 days, with a mean age at birth of 25.5 days [ab = 25.5 days]. This relatively protracted incubation is characteristic of species that lay large, yolk-rich eggs and may be linked to the thermal constraints of incubating on exposed, sandy substrates where maintaining a stable nest temperature is energetically demanding for the attending adults.

Following hatching, the young oystercatchers undergo a rapid phase of growth and feather development that culminates in fledging. Under the thermal regime typical of the species' active phase, which corresponds to an internal body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the time since birth at fledging is recorded as 35 days [tx = 35 days]. This relatively brief nestling period is characteristic of shorebirds that rely on early mobility to evade predators and begin foraging in the intertidal zone under parental guidance. The rapid acquisition of flight capabilities is critical, as it allows the fledgling to escape terrestrial threats and to commence independent feeding on benthic invertebrates. The fledging milestone is reached after a period of intensive parental provisioning, during which both adults deliver items such as cockles and mussels to the nest, ensuring that the growing chick accumulates sufficient energy reserves to sustain its first flights.

The attainment of sexual maturity occurs considerably later than fledging, reflecting the extended period required to develop the foraging skills and body condition necessary for successful reproduction. At a body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 105 days [tp = 105 days], a schedule that aligns well with the life histories of related shorebirds. This relatively early puberty, however, does not immediately translate into breeding activity; young oystercatchers often delay their first reproductive attempt for several years while they refine their foraging efficiency and secure a breeding territory. The onset of gonadal maturation at this stage marks the beginning of a prolonged period of social and ecological preparation, during which subadult birds frequently aggregate in non-breeding flocks along coastal stretches before eventually pairing and establishing a nesting site.

First reproduction, representing the commencement of actual breeding effort, is deferred relative to the age at puberty. Under the same thermal conditions (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]), the time since birth at first brood is recorded at 1095 days [tR = 1095 days]. This three-year delay between sexual maturation and the first successful nesting event is a well-documented feature of oystercatcher demography and is likely driven by intense competition for high-quality nesting territories on salt marshes and shell beaches. Females typically lay a clutch of approximately 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 3 eggs per clutch] and usually produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], yielding a modest annual reproductive output. This low reproductive rate is partially offset by a high degree of parental investment and a relatively long lifespan.

Longevity data for the genus Haematopus, derived from studies on the closely related species Haematopus bachmani, provide valuable context for understanding the population dynamics of H. ostralegus. At a body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 43.3 years [am = approximately 43.3 years], a remarkably extended longevity for a bird of this size. This long life span, combined with the deferred age at first breeding of 1095 days and the modest clutch size of 2 to 4 eggs, positions the Eurasian oystercatcher as a quintessential example of a slow life-history strategy among charadriiforms. Such a strategy is typically associated with environments where adult survival is high and juvenile mortality is unpredictable, allowing a long-lived individual to invest heavily in each reproductive event while maintaining the capacity to breed over many seasons.
